From An Owl
1. New Executive Director! I am delighted to inform you
that, after a long but fruitful search, the Executive Council
at its February meeting in Rochester, New York with the
Upsilon Chapter selected Mark A. Williams, Phi '76, as the
new Executive Director ofthe Fraternity. Mark will be join
ing us in Paoh on June 1. More biographical information on
Mark's background is included elsewhere in this issue of The
Diamond. Mark will be joining us as we lose the services of
our two superb Field Directors, Brian Gushing, Epsilon '89,
and T. J. Turner, Beta Beta '88. Their service to the Fraternity
has been marvelous and we will miss them but we wish them
well in their new endeavors.
Mark will be starting his tenure with the Fraternity at a
critical time in our history. Not only will he assist in the
implementation ofthe risk management standards that we all
understand to be so critical to the continued strength and
development of fraternities generally, but also he will assist
in the expansion that we have so long awaited in order to
assure the long term progress of our own Fraternity.
Mark has a long history of leadership in organizations in
volving volunteers. That volunteer leadership will provide
him with the skills necessary to motivate and lead our un
dergraduates and alumni as we move into a new phase of the
Fraternity's development.
AJ.. Psi Upsilon Leadership Institute. Probably the most
exciting single development for the long-term benefit of the
Fraternity is a project being jointly undertaken by the Fra
temity and the Foundation called the Psi Upsilon Leadership
Institute. The Institute will be held immediately before the
Convention in Atlanta this August. It will focus the attention
oftwo undergraduates from each chapter on the critical issues
of leadership facing our undergraduates generally and our
chapters specifically today. The focus of the Institute will be
the nine personal and professional ethical standards for un
dergraduate brothers developed by the National Interfra
ternity Conference's Commission on Ethics and Values.
Brother Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, current Executive Di
rector of the Psi Upsilon Foundation, serves as a member of
that Commission and has been the focal point with Tom Phil
lips, our Acting Executive Director, and our two Field Di
rectors in the development of the substantive agenda for the
Institute.
While many other fraternities have been able to develop
and conduct leadership institutes, some for many years, we
are delighted to be able finally to join our brother fraternities
in this meaningful activity. If it is as successful as we hope,
we intend to expand the Institute to include more under
graduates and alumni as funding permits and to increase the
amount of time available for such Institutes. We hope that
all of those undergraduates chosen to attend this year will
take back to their chapters the benefit of their experience.
HI. Expansion. As this column goes to press, the Exec
utive Council may well have acted to create three new pro
visional chapters �
one at Miami University in Oxford, Ohio,
a second at the University of Texas in Austin, Texas, and a
third at Washington State University in Pullman, Washing
ton. Just the prospect of Psi Upsilon having three provisional
chapters at the same time is virtually unheard oil The level
of enthusiasm that exists within the staff and the undergrad
uate groups that are petitioning to become provisional chap
ters is high! Psi Upsilon a number of years ago determined
that the future economic viability of the Fraternity would be
secure if we were able to achieve a total of 40 active chapters.
The prospects for reaching that long sought goal are now
within our grasp if we can continue to attract undergraduates
who are ofthe caliber and attend institutions of higher learn
ing of the caliber of those we are now finding at our door.
IV. Convention in Adanta. Prepare now to join us in
Atlanta for the Convention to be held there following the
Leadership Institute on August 18-19, 1990. Our Presidentto-be Charles M. Hall, Nu Alpha '71, will, along with the
Gamma Tau Chapter be the host and looks foi-ward along with
all members of the Executive Council to welcoming you at
that time!
1 know that you all join me in welcoming Mark Williams
as our Executive Director as we embark upon this exciting
phase in our history. Mark's efforts will no doubt enhance
those that have been expended so faithfully by Henry Poor,
Kathy McGlone, and Tom Phillips in the recent past!
Yours in the bonds.
William R .
Robie,
Epsilon Omega '66 President

PSI U HOOTS
Fraternity News From Across the Continent
Phi Chapter House Burns, December 13, 1989
PHI FIRE
On December 13, 1989, a potentially
disastrous fire ripped through the Phi
Chapter house at the University of Mich
igan. The blaze occurred on the eve of
exam week and was believed to have been
caused by the use of a hght bulb of the
wrong wattage in a bedroom lamp.
The fire left a large hole in the roof
and considerable water damage in the
house. Thanks however, to the heroic ef
forts of Phi Alumni Association President
Ed Spence '58, repairs were
underway
almost immediately. Brother Spence is a
partner in the Spence Brothers construc
tion firm and was fortunately in Ann Ar
bor at the time of the fire, working on
the new $12 million athletic facility at the
University of Michigan. Construction re
pair crews worked continually on the
house and, as a result, the undergraduate
brothers were back living in the house
one month later.
We all send a hearty Psi, Psi, Psi to
Brother Spence and the Phi undergrad
uates for their perseverance and deter
mination.
1990-91 UNDERGRADUATE
ADVISORY BOARD
The 1990-91 Undergraduate Advisory
Board has recently been elected. The sixbrother team of undergraduate leaders
will now prepare to meet with the Ex
ecutive Council in June and later to play
a
leading role in the 147th Convention.
The UAB will elect a Chairman and ViceChairman at their June meeting and these
two will serve as fiall voting members and
the undergraduate voice on Psi Upsilon's
Executive Council for the year. Con
gratulations to each new member of the
Undergraduate Advisory Board: Scott
Thomas, Zeta Tau '91; Jonathan W. Gar
diner, Psi '92; Mark Calabrese, Eta '91;
Bedford H. Lydon, III, Phi Beta '92;
James F. Probst, Epsilon Nu '91; Carl
W. Schmid, III, Epsilon '91.
FIRST EVER LEADERSHIP
INSTITUTE
Undergraduates heading south to At
lanta and the Gamma Tau Chapter this
August wall enjoy more than just the 147th
Convention. For the first time in Psi Up
silon's history, the Convention will be
preceded by the Psi Upsilon Leadership
Institute.
Designed to enable chapter leaders to
more clearly focus on the challenging is
sues facing today's undergraduates, the
Leadership Institute will be held on Au
gust 16-17, and will immediately be fol
lowed by the 147th Convention, August
18-19. The Leadership Institute will in
volve the participation of leaders within
Psi Upsilon's ranks, as well as university
and fratemity experts. Both events will
be held at the beautiful Ritz-Carlton in
Atlanta's Buckhead section.
RISKY BUSINESS
For the past two years THE topic
among Convention delegates and all un
dergraduates has been risk management.
Since Psi Upsilon joined with twentyseven other fraternities in the Fraternity
Insurance Purchasing Group (F.I.P.G.)
in 1988, we have been forced to reassess
every facet of chapter operations from
kitchen operations to social functions. Al
though the topic has been preeminent in
fraternity affairs, there has not been a
comprehensive program to implement
our new standards . . . until now.
At this summer's 147th Convention in
Atlanta, the Psi Upsilon Risk Manage
ment Manual will be unveiled. Hundreds
of man hours have been put into this tool
which will provide our chapters with a
comprehensive and practical Risk Man
agement Program. This new manual will
be a vital resource for every chapter. Psi
Upsilon hopes to move forward by get
ting back to the basics of common sense
and responsibility as we forge ahead into
a new decade.
FALL OF THE HOUSE OF
VANDERBILT
Psi Upsilon was mentioned in a recent
book Fortunes Children the Fall of the
House of Vanderbilt . The book is about
the accumulation (and subsequent
spending) of this family's famous fortune.
One of the members of the family, Wil
ham Henry Vanderbilt, II, was noted as
being a member of Psi Upsilon at Yale.

The Williams' Family �
Alec, Mariann, Evan, and Mark
Mark A. Williams, Phi '76
On February 24, 1990, Psi Upsi
lon's Executive Council unanimously
voted to name Mark A. Williams, Phi
'76, Executive Director of Psi Upsi
lon Fraternity. An attorney for the
law offices of Kern and Woolsey in
Mesa, Arizona, husband, and father
of two, Brother Williams will take
the reigns from Acting Executive Di
rector Thomas L. Phillips, Omicron
'85, on June 1, 1990.
After graduating with distinction
from the University of Michigan in
1976, Brother Williams then went on
to the University of Detroit School
of Law, where he was awarded his
Juris Doctor degree in 1979. Follow
ing his graduation from law school,
Mark went on to Phoenix, Arizona,
where he served a clerkship at the
Arizona Supreme Court before join
ing the firm ofWeyl, Guyer, MacBan
& Olson, P. A. in 1981, engaging in
general civil trial and appellate prac
tice.
In 1987, Brother Williams became
a Corporate Litigation Attorney for
Sentry Insurance in Scottsdale, Ari
zona. While with Sentry Insurance,
Mark was responsible for obtaining
and overseeing services rendered by
outside counsel in the western United
States. A year later Brother Williams
joined his current employer, the
multi-state firm of Kern and Wooley
in Mesa, Arizona, where his practice
has been focused on insurance de
fense.
Brother Williams remains active
with his alma mater, formerly serv
ing as the President ofthe University
of Michigan Club of Greater Phoenix
and currently serving as the Presi
dent of the University's Alumni As
sociation 8th District Clubs Council.
Mark's interests include swimming,
bicycling, and running, and in that
order Mark has been a two-time fin
isher of the Hawaii Ironman Triath
lon.
As Mark heads east to the friendly
confines of Paoli, Pennsylvania, he
brings with him his wife Mariann,
also a graduate of the University of
Michigan and member of Alpha Delta
Pi Sorority, and their two sons Evan,
age four, and Alec, age three.
Brother Williams recently dis
cussed this new opportunity for him
self, his family, and his fi-atemity with

of PSI UPSILON 5
members of The DIAMOND staff.
Excerpts from the conversation have
been printed for alumni and under
graduates to have a better look at the
man who will lead Psi Upsilon's staff
in the 1990s.
Q) How/why did you become in
terested in Psi U's Executive Direc
tor position?
A) Over the years I have served
on a number of volunteer boards and
on each board I gravitated toward the
projects or programs which permit
ted direct contact with students.
Probably the single most exciting
thing about becoming the Executive
Director of Psi Upsilon is the oppor
tunity to work with the undergrad
uate members of our fratemity. Every
alumnus who volunteers time and ef
fort on behalf of the fraternity does
so because he enjoys and is stimu
lated by the undergraduates. The
quality of our undergraduate mem
bers, the collective character of the
group, as well as the potential for
achievement is invigorating.
I also look forward to interacting
with our alumni. I never cease to be
amazed at how, after a ten minute
conversation with a brother I had
never met previously, I feel as if I
have a
lifelong friend. The fraternity
spans so many generations, it is al
ways remarkable to find the common
experiences among us and hear about
the unique adventures of individual
brothers.
Finally, I am absolutely thrilled to
have the opportunity to travel to the
various colleges and universities at
which we have chapters. I am for
tunate to have travelled extensively
in the West, both professionally and
for pleasure, and in each city I usu
ally managed to find my way to the
local college or university for a look
around.
Q) Why would you leave the law
profession to work for a fraternity?
A) One of the benefits of a liberal
arts education is flexibility. My un
dergraduate degree is in English and
was followed by a law degree. As a
litigator I have had some wonderful
opportunities, met some unique peo
ple, and have been greatly chal
lenged. I have done my share ofjury
trials and after eleven years of prac
ticing law, I want some different
challenges.
I fully expect that after my second
career with Psi Upsilon, there will
be a third career in an area that I
probably don't even know exists now.
Ten years ago if you would have told
me that on June 1, 1990, I would be
the Executive Director of Psi Upsi
lon, I would not have believed it.
Q) Based on what you have seen
of Psi U as an international frater
nity, is there anything in particular
you'll want to address immediately?
A) I see three areas which require
immediate attention. The first is the
diversification ofour income sources.
The international fraternity exists as
the result of the extraordinary gen
erosity of our alumni. We receive
more contributions, from a greater
percentage of alumni, and in greater
individual amounts, than any other
fraternity of which I am aware.
Nevertheless, there is a limit to such
generosity and I think we are chal
lenged to find additional sources of
revenue without resorting to an overt
commercialization of the Psi Upsilon
name.
I would also like to strengthen our
alumni organization. We have many
exceptional chapter corporations
which are lead by extraordinary in
dividuals. In those communities
where we have a chapter and such a
chapter corporation exists, our alumni
are well served; nevertheless, there
are many areas across the country
where we have large concentrations
of alumni who would like to be ac
tively involved in the fraternity but
may not be able to attend a conven
tion. Southern California, as well as
Dallas and Houston are areas where
we have a good number of alumni
who we do not reach. I would like to
build an alumni services program to
complement our chapter services ef
forts.
And, of course, there is our risk
management program.
Q) Getting more specific, what do
you think of all of the attention that
risk management is receiving?
A) Operating a fraternity chapter
house is a very sophisticated en
deavor. A chapter is at once a resi
dence hotel, a restaurant, a learning
center, and a social club. Without a
risk management plan we simply
cross our fingers and hope that all
goes well. Psi Upsilon has developed
a sophisticated risk management pro
gram which does nothing more than
endeavor to make our fratemity a safe
place to live, work, and socialize.
The Psi Upsilon Risk Management
Program was designed to meet the
needs ofour individual chapters. Suf
fice it to say that the risk manage
ment standards have not been openly
embraced by several of our chapters
and chapter corporations. It is a mis
take and very short sighted to say
that the imposition of a risk manage
ment program stems from the whim
of an insurance company or an over
cautious Executive Council.
There are those who feel that man
datory seat belt laws are burdensome
and an imposition on individual lib
erty; however, I don't think there are
too many people who can seriously
argue that mandatory child restraint
seats are unreasonable. Property in
surers generally require smoke de
tectors and fire extinguishers in our
homes, while hospitals have multivolume policy and procedure man
uals which are simply risk manage
ment programs. We address risk
management issues in our homes and
work places, why shouldn't the Fra
ternity address it?
Risk management has been called
a survival issue; that is, without it the
fraternity will not survive in light of
all the factors facing fraternities to
day. I look at it as a prosperity issue.
With sound risk management pro
grams in all of our chapters, we can
go to individual colleges and univer
sities and say these are the steps we
are taking to ensure the health and
safety of our members, our guests,
the communities in which they exist,
and the colleges and universities
where they are found. In the event
of an unfortunate occurrence, I would
much prefer to say that we did every
thing we could reasonably do to pre
vent the incident, rather than to be
in the position where I would have
to say we simply crossed our fingers
and hoped for the best.

6
Q) Psi Upsilon is also investigating
several possible changes to the
pledge education program. What are
your thoughts on these possible
changes and how much attention will
it receive in the near future?
A) Having served on the Task Force
on Brotherhood, I have had the op
portunity to review a number of al
ternatives to what has come to be
known as the traditional pledge pro
gram. I think we will see changes in
the pledge education process in the
very near future and I think it is going
to happen for a couple of reasons.
The first reason is hazing. Even
with the tremendous attention haz
ing has received over the last several
years, as well as the unequivocal
stance against hazing taken by the
National Interfraternity Conference,
the individual fraternities, and the
Executive Council of Psi Upsilon, a
traditional pledge program provides
the opportunity for hazing to occur.
There is certainly less outright phys
ical abuse than there once was, but
hazing is now more sophisticated and
subtle. We are
talking about the risk
we run when we put one group of
members in a subservient role to an
other group. Surely there must be a
better way to meet our
membership
education goals.
The other issue that we face has
nothing to do with hazing. Anyone
interested in secondary education
knows that the demographers are
telling us that the pool of candidates
for our
colleges and universities is
changing drastically. The overall
group of students who will be enter
ing colleges and universities in the
next ten years is getting smaller, its
composition is more diverse, and, at
the schools where Psi Upsilon exists,
the group is going to be more tal
ented. We will have a smaller field
of candidates from which to draw our
members than was available to us over
the past twenty years. The schools at
which our chapters are found are
highly selective and the students who
find their way to those colleges and
universities vdll be more gifted and
more talented than they are today.
As a result, the competition for these
students will be intense. If those pro
spective members perceive our
pledge education process as out
dated, we will lose those individuals
to the rugby team, the glee club, the
math club, or whatever organization
it is that these individuals feel most
closely serves their purposes. The re
cruitment of new members to Psi
Upsilon is going to become an ever
more sophisticated effort.
Psi Upsilon has prospered on many
campuses where other fraternities
have failed largely as a result of our
willingness to respond to the chang
ing climate at our colleges and uni
versities as well as our openness to
new ideas. While my role as Exec
utive Director is to implement policy
established by the Executive Council
and legislated at our conventions, I
personally advocate a system where
we immediately grant full rights and
privileges of membership to individ
uals who accept a bid. Thereafter, I
would undertake a member educa
tion program which requires all
members to know the lore and tra
ditions of our fraternity, actively to
support house functions, and to ac
cept responsibility for the mainte
nance and upkeep of the physical
property. I would preserve the big
brother/little brother tradition which
would pair a new member with an
upperclassman who would serve as a
mentor. Every task required of the
little brother would also be required
of the big brother. This type of pro
gram would serve to develop a sense
of unity within the brotherhood as
well as to create the sense of respon
sibility and commitment desirable in
our organization.
Q) Moving away from the present
tense, and speaking philosophically,
where do you see Psi U and the na
ture of all fraternities five, ten, or
twenty years from now?
A) I pledged Psi Upsilon in 1971
when fraternities in general were at
their lowest ebb. There were less than
150,000 undergraduate members of
fraternities when I became a Psi U.
Today, there are more than 400,000
undergraduate members of fratemi
ties and I am hopeful that we have
not yet reached the high water mark.
In five years I would like to have
begun an expansion process in which
we have targeted those colleges and
universities whose admissions poli
cies are considered selective. I would
like to improve our outreach to the
alumni and I am hopeful that we can
develop a leadership institute for both
our undergraduates and alumni and
present the program on a regional
basis. In ten years I would like to see
a permanent international headquar
ters facility. In twenty years I want
Psi Upsilon to be the model for a
college fraternity which prepares its
members to prosper in a twenty-first
century where they will find a multi
cultural, ethnically diverse, plural
istic society where knowledge is the
stock in trade. Fraternities began as
literary societies, and in the eyes of
some, came to be viewed as nothing
more than drinking clubs. As an or
ganization of educated people, Psi
Upsilon is ideally situated to promote
higher education, to encourage val
ues and ethics in society, and to serve
our respective communities.
Q) Do you have any other per
sonal plans or goals at this point for
yourself and/or Psi U?
A) When I pledged at the Phi
Chapter of Psi Upsilon, I did so be
cause I considered it to be the best
fraternity in Ann Arbor, it certainly
had the most impressive house on
campus, and I then felt intuitively
rather than intellectually that it was
the best place for me. I am humbled
to follow in the footsteps ofthose who
have come before me as Executive
Director. I marvel at the manner in
which the Executive Council has
been able to find the right individual
to lead the fraternity at the various
stages of its history, I am hopeful that
there will come a day when that can
be said about me.
As a parent your perspective
changes a little and you tend to view
things in light of your children. I have
sons who are now three and four years
old and I am hopeful that they will
be able to attend a selective college,
and ifthere is a chapter of Psi Upsilon
there, I would like my sons to be
come my fraternity brothers. It is my
hope that they choose Psi Upsilon,
not because of what their father did,
but because a particular chapter was
the best fraternity on campus, with
the most impressive brothers, and
which best filled their needs.

THE CHAPTERS REPORT
THETA
1833
Union College
This year has been quite prosperous at
the Theta. We have participated in areas
which were
previously foreign to us, while
simultaneously raising our GPA to chal
lenge all ofthe other Greeks. The school's
social policy has substantially changed,
but we are coping with these changes as
best as possible. Along with these
changes, also came the addition of eight
new pledges. We feel these young men
possess the characteristic that can uphold
the standards and morals on which our
fratemity relies.
Throughout the year the Theta has
participated in various types of commu
nity service. First and foremost, we have
helped the nearby Baker Street Boy's
Club begin a "Smart Moves" program.
The program deals with alcohol, drug,
and sexual abuse at an early age. We have
sponsored a ski boot sale as well as a pool
tournament to raise money to help these
deserved children. As a house we have
also brought the kids to a Union hockey
game which the youngsters very much
appreciated.
The chapter is anxiously awaiting the
arrival of spring term and the opportunity
to rid ourselves of the eternal gloom of
winter. But, meanwhile our intramural
hockey team is searching for its' second
title in the past two years.
Elections are rapidly approaching and
the authority and governance of the fra
ternity will soon change hands. The
chapter is operating as efiiciently as ever
and we are confident that will continue
to do so in the future.
Nicholas Baratoff IV '90
Past President
KAPPA
1843
Bowdoin College
The 1989-90 school year has been a
dynamic and productive time at the Kappa
Chapter. With a new fi-atemity standards
report completed by the Bowdoin admin
istration and our
Interfraternity Council,
many new demands and challenges have
been made on all fratemities. The Kappa
chapter has played a vital role in the
forming of this document and has led the
fratemities in adopting the new policies.
With a balanced ratio of men to women
Kappa Chapter House, Bowdoin College
and many campus leaders among us, the
Kappa Chapter has shown other frater
nities and the administration that an en
vironment of equality and diversity is,
and always has been, our aim.
All of the fraternities have responded
extremely well to the strict new alcohol
policies the state and the administration

ebration of the Chapter House and the

quest the honor of hosting Psi Upsilon's

to briefly update the Xi Alumni on the
issue of what appears to be the imminent
coeducation of Wesleyan's all-male fra
temities.
In 1987, the President's Residential
Life Task Force Report established a three
year period in which Wesleyan's four re
maining all-male fraternities, Psi Upsi
lon, Beta Theta Pi, Delta Kappa Epsilon,
and Chi Psi would be persuaded to coeducate their memberships. During this
time, Psi Upsilon has been asked to jus
tify its existence in the context of a fully
co-educated academic environment. As
undergraduates we met this challenge last
fall with a detailed document defending
our right to free association (each of you
should have received a copy of Psi U's
response dated 10-20-89). Now that 1990
has arrived, President Chace has decided
to abandon the methods ofpersuasion for
a more aggressive approach of coercion.

committed to preserving the institution
which has continually provided us with
the support, love, and friendship that the
University itself has failed to offer. We
believe that there is nothing inherently
immoral about all-male institutions, and
strongly feel that the valuable benefits
derived from an all-male membership sit
uation would cease to exist if coeducation
were forced upon us.
In view of the current lack of centrally
located housing for Wesleyan's female
students, we cannot help but feel that
the all-male fratemities have become a
scapegoat for the University's lack of
foresight in anticipating the overwhelm
ing growth in student enrollment over
the past fifteen years. In my mind, Wes
leyan's plan to co-educate the fi-atemities
appears to be nothing more than a shortterm solution to a long-term problem.
Wesleyan has always prided itself on
the wide variety of choices it has to offer.
Over the past eighteen months, how
ever, many of these options have disappered. To avoid hypocrisy and unjust dis
crimination against the fraternities, the
current administration will, if committed
to its mission of full-scale coeducation.
be compelled to continue its eflForts until
all aspects of residential life are co-edu
cated. As members of both Psi Upsilon
and the Wesleyan Community, we ada
mantly oppose this forced coeducation of
the Xi or any other independent frater
nity. We sincerely hope that you will
continue to support our decisions re
garding membership, and ask that you
take a moment to address your concerns
about the issue of coeducation to Presi
dent William Chace, Wesleyan Univer
sity. Homogenization is not the answer.
Michael A . Huddleston '90

The Zeta Zeta Chapter of Psi Upsilon
headed into the University of British Co
lumbia's 75th year with strength and mo
mentum. After last year's success, cul
minating with UBC's "Most Improved
Fratemity" award, the brothers felt great
about the future. The start of the year
was hectic because of rush, but under the
guidance of our Rush Chairman, D.
Wayne Best '91, the chapter pledged 16
fine men, 14 of whom were initiated and
are a vital part of our growing chapter.
Once again, Psi Upsilon was imaginative
and lead by example, having a totally dry
rush.

force in UBC's intramural sports pro
gram. Victories are expected in volleyball
(lead by our power hitter Peter A. Marron '91) and our talented basketball team
is sure to successfiilly defend its title.

the ball hockey team and there is now a
strong chance of obtaining that champi
onship as well.

three new individual awards this year.

ecutive Council at the 132nd Annual Upsilon Chapter Initiation banquet.
